\begin{abstract}
Self-consistency yields large gains on discrete-answer tasks, but named entity recognition (NER) produces \textit{sets} of entities with partial overlap, where no majority vote analog exists.
We evaluate five confidence signals for quality estimation (QE) and sample selection on four NER benchmarks using fine-tuned 4B\textendash 8B models.
All signals achieve reliable QE ($\rho$ up to 0.50, area under the ROC curve [AUROC] up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
For instance-level selection, log-probability (LP) succeeds only where LP-quality alignment is strong, and gains are absent elsewhere despite large oracle headroom (the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}).
We diagnose two causes: instance degeneracy and weak LP-quality alignment; degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings but does not predict cross-dataset direction.
The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level \textit{construction}, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation improves F1 by $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$). Construction and LP selection are complementary, governed by LP-quality alignment.
\end{abstract}

1	\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}
2	
3	Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
4	But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.
5	
6	Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
7	Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
8	Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
9	Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.
10	
11	A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
12	All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.50, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
13	For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
14	On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
15	Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
16	Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
17	Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
18	Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.
19	
20	\begin{figure*}[t]
21	\centering
22	\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
23	\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its resolution. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.50; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
24	\label{fig:overview}
25	\end{figure*}
26	
27	We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
28	We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
29	An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
30	Our contributions:
31	\begin{enumerate}
32	    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
33	    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.50, AUROC up to 0.82).
34	    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
35	
36	    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
37	    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
38	    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.
39	
40	    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation.}
41	    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
42	    Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes datasets.
43	\end{enumerate}
44

\section{Introduction}\label{sec:introduction}

Self-consistency (majority voting over multiple samples) yields large gains on discrete-answer reasoning \citep{wang2023selfconsistency}, and test-time compute scaling has emerged as a complementary axis to model scaling \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys}.
But named entity recognition (NER) poses a structurally different challenge: the output is a \textit{set} of entities, two samples may extract overlapping but non-identical sets, and there is no obvious majority to vote on.

Prior work on confidence estimation for LLM-based IE has conflated \textit{quality estimation} (which inputs does the model handle reliably?) with \textit{sample selection} (which of $N$ outputs is best?).
Existing self-consistency methods \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, chen2024usc, taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty} assume outputs can be grouped by equivalence, an assumption that breaks for entity sets with partial overlap.
Unlike \citet{yao2026consistency}, who demonstrate that self-consistency correlates with task accuracy, we provide the first systematic empirical characterization of \textit{when and why} LP-based selection succeeds or fails for structured prediction, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as the two blocking mechanisms.
Our experiments use fine-tuned models, the dominant deployment paradigm for production NER, and separate quality estimation from best-of-$N$ selection.

A key distinction structures our analysis: four of five signals (Soft Jaccard, voting confidence, Fleiss' $\kappa$, exact match) are instance-level aggregates that assign identical scores to all $N$ candidates for a given input; only log-probability (LP) is natively per-sample.
All signals achieve reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.50, AUROC up to 0.82; Figure~\ref{fig:overview}), supporting selective prediction.
For selection, LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) in settings where both low instance degeneracy and adequate alignment are present, with gains scaling with $N$.
On SciERC, the observed LP gain ($+0.2$~pp, $p{=}0.29$) falls below the minimum detectable effect (${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power, $n{=}529$) despite 13~pp oracle headroom. We term this disparity between quality estimation strength and selection effectiveness the \textbf{correlation-selection gap}.
Two factors shape this gap: (a)~\textit{instance degeneracy}, the fraction of instances where all $N$ samples produce identical F1, (13\textendash 87\% across our benchmarks) limits the available headroom; (b)~\textit{LP-quality alignment} (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) determines whether LP can exploit the remaining headroom (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Our diagnosis is complementary to minimum Bayes risk (MBR) utility misalignment \cite{eikema2025structured}: where MBR failures in structured prediction stem from poorly chosen utility functions, we find that degeneracy eliminates candidate diversity before utility alignment matters.
Within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Both mechanisms intensify with model capability: degeneracy rises with scale and training convergence (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). This creates a tension between model quality and test-time improvability.

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_overview}
\caption{Overview of the correlation-selection gap and its resolution. \textbf{Left}: consistency signals reliably estimate instance-level quality ($\rho$ up to 0.50; Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}). \textbf{Center}: instance-level signals assign identical scores to all samples from the same input, so best-of-$N$ selection cannot outperform greedy. \textbf{Right}: entity-level construction aggregates entities across samples via majority vote ($\theta{=}2/N$), bypassing the selection bottleneck ($+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD, multi-seed mean; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).}
\label{fig:overview}
\end{figure*}

We evaluate five signals from three families (structural, surface, and model-internal) on SciERC \cite{luan2018scierc} as a primary medium-difficulty test bed, with Few-NERD \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (low-degeneracy contrast), CoNLL-2003 \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (ceiling-effect control), and WNUT-17 \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (signal-collapse boundary), using two 8B models (Qwen3-8B, LLaMA-3.1-8B) with a 4B ablation (Qwen3-4B).
We vary candidate pool size ($N{\in}\{2,\ldots,32\}$), signal sophistication, and model capacity within the 4B\textendash 8B range; behavior at 70B+ scales remains an open question.
An exploratory extension to relation extraction is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Our contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{Quality estimation framework and selective prediction.}
    Five signals from three families evaluated on four NER benchmarks, two model families, and a 4B ablation, achieving reliable quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.50, AUROC up to 0.82).
    QE enables selective prediction: filtering low-confidence instances at 80\% coverage yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (area under the precision-recall curve [AUPRC] 0.70--0.92, VC strongest; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).

    \item \textbf{Diagnostic of the correlation-selection gap.}
    For fine-tuned 4B--8B models, LP-quality alignment (within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$) is the primary predictor of selection success: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{<}0.001$) where alignment is strong, but not on benchmarks with weak alignment.
    Instance degeneracy causally modulates LP within fixed settings (epoch and temperature ablations), but does not predict cross-dataset direction ($\rho{=}0.052$, 23 configurations); structural signals fail by construction; supervised combinations and hidden state probes (Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}) confirm the gap persists.

    \item \textbf{Entity-level construction as a diagnostic-motivated mitigation.}
    The diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level aggregation, adapting entity voting from ensemble NER \cite{florian2003named} to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted construction yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$; \S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
    Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets, governed by LP-quality alignment; a simple alignment-based gating protocol correctly routes datasets.
\end{enumerate}

1	\section{Experiments}
2	\label{sec:experiments}
3	
4	\subsection{Experimental Setup}
5	\label{sec:setup}
6	
7	\paragraph{Datasets.}
8	We evaluate on four English NER benchmarks spanning a difficulty gradient, each serving a distinct role.
9	\textbf{SciERC} \cite{luan2018scierc} (551 test instances, 6 entity types) is the primary medium-difficulty test bed where models achieve ${\approx}$65\% F1.
10	\textbf{Few-NERD} \cite{ding2021fewnerd} (INTRA coarse; 37{,}648 instances, 8 entity types, ${\approx}$75\% F1) provides a low-degeneracy contrast where LP selection succeeds (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}).
11	\textbf{CoNLL-2003} \cite{tjongkimsang2003conll} (3{,}453 test sentences, 4 entity types, ${\approx}$91\% F1) serves as a ceiling-effect control where limited oracle headroom constrains selection gains.
12	\textbf{WNUT-17} \cite{derczynski2017wnut} (1{,}287 social media instances, 52\% zero F1) probes the signal-collapse boundary where model capability is insufficient.
13	
14	\paragraph{Models and sampling.}
15	\textbf{Qwen3-8B} and \textbf{LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct} are LoRA fine-tuned using LLaMA Factory \cite{zheng2024llamafactory} (training details in Appendix~\ref{app:training}; Few-NERD uses 3 epochs vs.\ 5 for others due to earlier convergence; Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
16	We draw $N{=}8$ samples at $T{=}1.0$ (primary) with vLLM constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided}, with $N{=}16$ for scaling experiments (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
17	
18	%% ============================================================
19	\subsection{Quality Estimation Results}
20	\label{sec:qe_results}
21	
22	\begin{table*}[t]
23	\centering
24	\small
25	\caption{NER quality estimation ($\rho$ and AUROC; $N{=}8$, primary seed${=}42$; 3-seed stability $\sigma{\leq}0.026$ in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}). Best in \textbf{bold}. RE results in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}. $N{=}16$ in Table~\ref{tab:robustness}.}
26	\label{tab:quality_estimation}
27	\begin{tabular}{ll cc cc cc}
28	\toprule
29	& & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{SciERC}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (Qwen)}} & \multicolumn{2}{c}{\textbf{CoNLL (LLaMA)}} \\
30	\cmidrule(lr){3-4} \cmidrule(lr){5-6} \cmidrule(lr){7-8}
31	Signal & Family & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC & $\rho$ & AUC \\
32	\midrule
33	VC & Structural & \textbf{.379} & \textbf{.663} & .424 & .789 & .426 & .709 \\
34	SJ  & Structural & .360 & .650 & .436 & .801 & \textbf{.431} & .704 \\
35	FK & Surface & .267 & .602 & .400 & .774 & .428 & .703 \\
36	EM  & Surface    & .295 & .614 & \textbf{.451} & \textbf{.816} & \textbf{.431} & .705 \\
37	\midrule
38	LP     & Model      & .205 & .578 & .316 & .753 & .307 & \textbf{.761} \\
39	\bottomrule
40	\end{tabular}
41	\end{table*}
42	
43	Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation} presents $\rho$ and AUROC for five signals across tasks and models ($\varepsilon$-free; $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ applies to selection only, stable across $[0, 0.2]$, Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}).
44	
45	\paragraph{Signal rankings are difficulty-dependent.}
46	On SciERC (medium difficulty), structural signals lead (VC $\rho{=}0.379$, SJ $0.360$) over LP ($0.205$); bootstrap CIs confirm the gap ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.155$; Appendix~\ref{app:bootstrap_signal}).
47	On CoNLL (single-sample F1${\approx}$0.91), EM leads both $\rho$ and AUROC ($0.816$).
48	At the signal-collapse boundary (WNUT-17, macro F1${\approx}$42\%), full-set correlations are dominated by the zero/non-zero boundary (VC $\rho{=}0.724$ but conditional $\rho{=}0.038$; Table~\ref{tab:wnut}); LP shows the reverse (conditional $\rho{=}0.350$; Figure~\ref{fig:signal_heatmap}).
49	This collapse illustrates a regime where model capability is insufficient to produce meaningful inter-sample variation: 52\% of instances yield zero F1 across all samples, and consistency signals merely detect this floor rather than discriminating quality among non-trivial outputs.
50	
51	%% ============================================================
52	\subsection{The Correlation-Selection Gap}
53	\label{sec:selection_gap}
54	
55	Four of five signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) assign identical scores to all candidates from the same input by construction (\S\ref{sec:formulation}); they can estimate quality across instances but cannot rank candidates within an instance.
56	The empirical question is whether LP, the sole per-sample signal, can exploit its candidate-discriminative nature for selection.
57	LP selection effectiveness is primarily determined by LP-quality alignment rather than degeneracy level (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
58	Cross-instance $\rho$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}) is attenuated by varying instance difficulty; within-instance $\rho$ directly measures whether LP discriminates candidates for a fixed input, making it the relevant predictor of selection success.
59	
60	\begin{table}[t]
61	\centering
62	\small
63	\caption{Best-of-$N$ NER selection (macro F1) on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$). LP is per-sample; others use consensus-proximity. Best non-oracle in \textbf{bold}. Non-tied subset in \S\ref{sec:discussion}; RE in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}. $^\dagger$Instance-level signals assign one score per input; per-sample ranking $p$-values are undefined.}
64	\label{tab:selection}
65	\begin{tabular}{lcc}
66	\toprule
67	Method & NER F1 & $p$ \\
68	\midrule
69	Oracle & $0.775 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
70	Greedy ($T{=}0$) & $0.645 \pm 0.001$ & --- \\
71	\midrule
72	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Per-sample signal}} \\
73	LP           & $\mathbf{0.647} \pm 0.005$ & .29 \\
74	\midrule
75	\multicolumn{3}{l}{\textit{Instance-level signals (consensus-proximity selection)}} \\
76	SJ           & $0.646 \pm 0.002$ & .67 \\
77	FK           & $0.646 \pm 0.001$ & .79 \\
78	EM           & $0.637 \pm 0.001$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
79	VC           & $0.623 \pm 0.004$ & n/a$^\dagger$ \\
80	\midrule
81	Random           & $0.610 \pm 0.003$ & --- \\
82	\bottomrule
83	\end{tabular}
84	\end{table}
85	
86	\begin{figure}[t]
87	\centering
88	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_selection_gap}
89	\caption{The correlation-selection gap on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, 2-seed mean). Bars show quality estimation $\rho$; the line with error bars shows $\Delta$F1 vs.\ greedy. Despite $\rho$ up to 0.36, no signal significantly outperforms greedy (all $p{>}0.05$; Table~\ref{tab:selection}). Dashed green: oracle upper bound ($+13.1$~pp); dotted gray: random baseline.}
90	\label{fig:selection_gap}
91	\end{figure}
92	
93	Instance-level signals assign identical QE scores to all candidates; MBR conversion does not improve over greedy on the primary test bed (Table~\ref{tab:selection}; Figure~\ref{fig:selection_gap}).
94	Instance-level signals predict \textit{which inputs} the model handles reliably, not \textit{which output} is best.
95	
96	\paragraph{LP: the sole per-sample signal also fails.}
97	On SciERC ($n{=}529$, 2-seed sign tests\footnote{MDE${\approx}$1.5~pp at 80\% power ($n{=}529$); Few-NERD ($n{=}32{,}565$; MDE${\approx}$0.22~pp) provides the definitive test.}), the oracle (0.775) reveals 13.0~pp of headroom, but LP achieves $+0.2$~pp ($p{=}0.29$), below the MDE (${\approx}$1.5~pp); selection effects below this threshold cannot be reliably detected.
98	The pattern holds across CoNLL and WNUT-17 (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}); under stringent TOST anchors, some configurations show significant \textit{degradation} (Appendix~\ref{app:tost}).
99	Few-NERD provides the definitive contrast: LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$) at low degeneracy (\S\ref{sec:fewnerd}), while structural signals still degrade selection.
100	
101	\paragraph{Expected selection gain decomposition.}
102	The expected selection gain can be approximately factored as $\mathbb{E}[\Delta\text{F1}] \approx (1 - d) \cdot \Delta_{\text{oracle}} \cdot g(\rho_{\text{within}})$, where $d$ is the degeneracy rate, $\Delta_{\text{oracle}}$ is the oracle headroom, and $g$ is assumed monotonically increasing in within-instance LP-F1 correlation $\rho_{\text{within}}$, reflecting that stronger alignment enables more informative candidate ranking.
103	This decomposition is consistent with the observed data: SciERC ($d{=}17.8\%$, $\Delta_{\text{oracle}}{=}13.1$\,pp, $\rho_{\text{within}}{=}0.262$) predicts a small gain (actual: $+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp, 3-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}); Few-NERD ($d{=}13.8\%$, $\Delta_{\text{oracle}}{\approx}8$\,pp, $\rho_{\text{within}}{=}0.667$) predicts the largest gain (actual: $+1.39$\,pp); CoNLL ($d{=}48.4\%$, $\Delta_{\text{oracle}}{\approx}2$\,pp, low $\rho_{\text{within}}$) predicts near-zero gain (actual: $-0.85$\,pp).
104	The high SciERC seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.48$\,pp) reflects weak LP-quality alignment ($\rho{\approx}0.26$), consistent with the bound predicting unreliable selection.
105	
106	%% ============================================================
107	\subsection{Cross-Dataset Contrast: Few-NERD}
108	\label{sec:fewnerd}
109	
110	\begin{table}[t]
111	\centering
112	\small
113	\caption{LP selection across datasets (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, gold-filtered). Degen.\%: fraction with identical F1 across all samples. $p$: paired bootstrap vs.\ greedy. Few-NERD/CoNLL: 3-seed means; SciERC: single-seed (3-seed: $+0.04{\pm}0.48$~pp; Table~\ref{tab:multiseed}). Protocol details in \S\ref{sec:evaluation}; epoch choices in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.}
114	\label{tab:fewnerd}
115	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
116	\begin{tabular}{@{}lrccccr@{}}
117	\toprule
118	Dataset & $n$ & Greedy & Degen.\% & LP $\rho$ & LP $\Delta$ & $p$ \\
119	\midrule
120	CoNLL & 2{,}756 & .908 & 48.4\% & .302 & $-$0.85\,pp & 1.0 \\
121	SciERC & 529 & .644 & 17.8\% & .205 & $+$0.61\,pp & .193 \\
122	Few-NERD & 32{,}565 & .748 & 13.8\% & .220 & $\mathbf{+1.39}$\,pp & ${<}.001$ \\
123	\bottomrule
124	\end{tabular}}
125	\end{table}
126	
127	Few-NERD (Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}) confirms that LP selection effectiveness is inversely associated with degeneracy.
128	Under standard early stopping, Few-NERD degeneracy is 13.8\% and LP achieves $+1.39$~pp ($p{<}0.001$), while all structural signals degrade selection (VC $-1.79$, SJ $-2.14$~pp); LP is 50$\times$ more seed-stable ($\sigma{=}0.04$ vs.\ SJ $2.02$~pp) and generalizes to LLaMA-3.1-8B (Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
129	Training convergence modulates degeneracy: 5-epoch Few-NERD raises degeneracy to 31\% and halves LP gains (Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}).
130	
131	\paragraph{Degeneracy alone does not predict LP selection direction.}
132	Across 23 configurations, degeneracy does not predict LP gain ($\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$; Figure~\ref{fig:degeneracy_scatter}), though within fixed settings it causally modulates LP (Few-NERD per-entity-type $\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}).
133	Cross-dataset prediction requires LP signal quality: Few-NERD (within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$) shows consistent gains, while SciERC ($\rho{\approx}0.26$, even at matched duration $\rho{=}0.319$; Table~\ref{tab:epoch_scierc}) does not.
134	Conditional analysis on the favorable subset yields $+2.47$~pp on SciERC but remains negative on CoNLL (Appendix~\ref{app:conditional_decomp}).
135	
136	\begin{figure}[t]
137	\centering
138	\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig_degeneracy_lp_scatter.pdf}
139	\caption{Instance degeneracy vs.\ LP selection gain across 23 configurations ($N{=}8$; $\rho{=}0.052$, $p{=}0.81$). Within Few-NERD per-entity-type analysis ($\rho{=}{-}0.881$; Appendix~\ref{app:per_type_lp}), degeneracy predicts LP gain when alignment is held constant.}
140	\label{fig:degeneracy_scatter}
141	\end{figure}
142	
143	LP selection gains scale with $N$ (Few-NERD $N{=}16$: $+0.52$~pp, $p{=}0.003$; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}); structural signals remain negative regardless of sample budget.
144	
145	%% ============================================================
146	\subsection{Robustness}
147	\label{sec:robustness_main}
148	
149	Consistency signals are robust across $T{\in}\{0.7, 1.0\}$ with sublinear $N$-scaling gains (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}); LP shows the largest temperature sensitivity ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$).
150	Signal rankings are stable across seeds (Kendall's $W{=}1.0$ at $N{=}8$; $m{=}3$ raters, interpret with caution given low $m$; exact $p{\approx}0.028$; Table~\ref{tab:ranking-stability}).
151	NER calibration is reasonable (ECE 0.069--0.096; Appendix~\ref{app:calibration}).
152

154	\centering

156	\caption{Scale ablation: Qwen3-8B vs.\ 4B NER quality estimation ($\rho$; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$). 8B values identical to Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}; 4B uses matched evaluation protocol. RE scale ablation in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.}
157	\label{tab:scale_ablation}
158	\begin{tabular}{@{}ll cc r@{}}
159	\toprule
160	& & \textbf{8B} & \textbf{4B} & $\Delta$ \\
161	\midrule
162	CoNLL & SJ & .436 & .422 & $-$.014 \\
163	      & FK & .400 & .418 & $+$.018 \\
164	SciERC & SJ & .360 & .422 & $+$.062 \\
165	       & FK & .267 & .326 & $+$.059 \\

170	\paragraph{Scale robustness.}
171	With Qwen3-4B (Table~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}), QE is comparable (mean $|\Delta\rho|{=}0.042$), yet selection remains below greedy despite 13.0~pp headroom. Task difficulty is a stronger predictor than model scale within the 3B--8B range (Appendix~\ref{app:llama3b}).
172	Degeneracy scales with capability: 8B shows 17.8\% vs.\ 4B's 10.4\% on SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:degeneracy}).
173	
174	\paragraph{LoRA-rank ablation.}
175	LoRA rank${=}8$ (vs.\ 32) lowers degeneracy to 7.2\% but LP remains below greedy ($\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1}){\approx}0.24$); temperature manipulation ($T{=}1.2$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) provides a cleaner diversity test, confirming that low degeneracy and adequate alignment are independently necessary.
176	
177	\paragraph{Supervised signal combination.}
178	Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest; 5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, $N{=}16$) and a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier encoding input-output pairs all fail to close the selection gap: selection F1 remains at or below greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:supervised_combination}).
179	
180	Hidden state probes (MLP on final-layer representations) achieve higher quality correlation than LP on SciERC ($\rho{=}0.388$ vs.\ $0.283$, $+37$\%) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\% vs.\ $+4.8$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}). The correlation-selection gap extends to model-internal representations.
181	
182	%% ============================================================
183	\subsection{Prescriptive Results}
184	\label{sec:prescriptive}
185	
186	The preceding sections establish that instance-level selection fails for structured IE. We now present two approaches that extract value from multi-sample generation without relying on sample ranking.
187	
188	\paragraph{Entity-level construction.}
189	Rather than selecting one of $N$ complete outputs, we aggregate entities across all samples. For each unique entity mention, we compute its LP-weighted or uniform frequency across $N$ samples and retain those exceeding a confirmation threshold $\theta{=}2/N$ (an entity is included if it appears in ${\geq}2$ of $N$ samples). This empirically robust default achieves the best or near-best F1 across all datasets, and the optimum is stable within $\theta \in [0.15, 0.35]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:theta_sweep}; $\theta{=}0.5$ majority baseline in Appendix~\ref{app:entity_merge}).
190	
191	\begin{table}[t]
192	\centering
193	\small
194	\caption{Entity-level construction vs.\ greedy decoding ($\Delta$ macro F1; $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B, multi-seed mean${\pm}\sigma$: 3 seeds SciERC, 4 seeds Few-NERD). LP: LP-weighted entity aggregation; Unif.: frequency-based. $\theta{=}2/N$ (default heuristic). $p$: seed-42 paired bootstrap vs.\ greedy; LP-weighted positive across all seeds. Best per dataset in \textbf{bold}.}
195	\label{tab:entity_construction}
196	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
197	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccc@{}}
198	\toprule
199	Dataset & Wt. & Greedy & Constr. & $\Delta$ & $p$ \\
200	\midrule
201	SciERC & LP & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $\mathbf{.656{\pm}.003}$ & $+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp & .004 \\
202	       & Unif. & $.646{\pm}.002$ & $.653{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.71$\,pp & .023 \\
203	\addlinespace
204	Few-NERD & LP & $.748$ & $\mathbf{.762{\pm}.005}$ & $+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp & ${<}.001$ \\
205	         & Unif. & $.748$ & $.756{\pm}.006$ & $+0.74{\pm}0.58$\,pp & .003 \\
206	\addlinespace
207	CoNLL & Unif. & .908 & .904 & $-0.39$\,pp & n.s. \\
208	\bottomrule
209	\end{tabular}}
210	\end{table}
211	
212	LP-weighted construction significantly improves over greedy on Few-NERD ($+1.40{\pm}0.51$\,pp, $p{<}0.001$) and SciERC ($+1.02{\pm}0.49$\,pp, $p{=}0.004$; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), with LP-weighted gains positive across all 7 seed-dataset combinations, recovering approximately 8\% (SciERC) and 11\% (Few-NERD) of oracle headroom. CoNLL shows no significant gain ($-0.39$\,pp), consistent with ceiling-regime degeneracy. The mechanism is recall-driven: aggregating low-frequency correct entities across samples recovers mentions that no single sample captures.
213	Construction gains scale with $N$: at $N{=}16$ on Few-NERD, $\Delta$ rises to $+1.32$\,pp (seed-42; Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}), as more samples provide broader entity coverage.
214	
215	\paragraph{Construction and LP selection are complementary.}
216	Construction dominates on SciERC ($+1.02$\,pp vs.\ LP selection $+0.04{\pm}0.48$\,pp, not significant), where LP-quality alignment is weak (within-instance $\rho{\approx}0.2$).
217	On Few-NERD, both methods yield comparable gains (construction $+1.40$\,pp, LP selection $+1.39$\,pp; Tables~\ref{tab:entity_construction}, \ref{tab:fewnerd}), where alignment is strong ($\rho{\approx}0.5$--$0.7$).
218	The gating criterion is LP-quality alignment: when alignment is weak, construction is the only effective strategy; when alignment is strong, both methods succeed.
219	
220	\paragraph{LP-alignment gating.}
221	We probe 50 held-out validation instances to estimate within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$. Above threshold $0.3$, LP selection is applied; below it, entity construction is used instead; when construction yields negative gain (as on CoNLL), the protocol defaults to greedy decoding. Adjusted $\rho$ scores on the dev split (SciERC $0.167$, CoNLL $0.065$, Few-NERD $0.516$) correctly route all three datasets, with dev-set routing matching test-set routing 3/3. This preliminary protocol requires further validation with larger validation sets. Two caveats apply: (a) the protocol is validated on three datasets with large inter-dataset margins; (b) on high-degeneracy datasets (CoNLL, valid ratio 22\%), the adjusted score magnitude is noisy but the routing decision remains robust due to wide margin from the $0.3$ threshold.
222	
223	\paragraph{Selective prediction.}
224	Orthogonal to construction, QE signals support selective prediction: at 80\% coverage, retaining high-confidence instances yields $+5$--$8$\,pp F1 (AUPRC 0.70--0.92; VC strongest on Qwen, model-dependent on LLaMA; Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection}).
225	When selection fails, QE scores route low-confidence instances to human review.
226

1	\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}
2	
3	The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
4	Two factors constrain selection: instance degeneracy (17.8--48.4\%) eliminates headroom, and LP compression (within-instance $\rho$ 0.262--0.667) prevents exploiting the remainder; within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
5	Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, surviving Bonferroni across 5 signals; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}). However, $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory evidence for LP compression's role in the selection bottleneck.
6	Temperature disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); degeneracy rises with model scale and training convergence (Tables~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), so the selection window narrows as models improve \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.
7	
8	\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
9	Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms ($+1.40$\,pp Few-NERD, $+1.02$\,pp SciERC, multi-seed mean; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), complementary with LP selection and governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
10	Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) fail to reliably beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
11	Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding; settings with greater output diversity may restore selection headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:when_selection_works}).
12

\section{Discussion}\label{sec:discussion}

The decoupling of $\rho$, AUROC, and selection F1 means single-metric evaluation risks selecting the wrong signal; effective selection likely requires content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, venktesh2025trust}.
Two factors constrain selection: instance degeneracy (17.8--48.4\%) eliminates headroom, and LP compression (within-instance $\rho$ 0.262--0.667) prevents exploiting the remainder; within non-degenerate instances, MBR utility correlates positively with F1 (SJ median $\rho{=}0.524$) \cite{eikema2022sampling}.
Where compression is mitigated (LP range ${\geq}0.05$, $n{=}210$), LP selection yields $+2.9$~pp ($p{=}0.004$, surviving Bonferroni across 5 signals; Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}). However, $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\text{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory evidence for LP compression's role in the selection bottleneck.
Temperature disentangles the two factors: at $T{=}1.2$, degeneracy drops to 14.9\% yet LP does not improve ($\rho{=}0.225$ vs.\ Few-NERD ${\sim}$0.5--0.7; Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy}); degeneracy rises with model scale and training convergence (Tables~\ref{tab:scale_ablation}, \ref{tab:epoch_confound}), so the selection window narrows as models improve \cite{wang2023selfconsistency, snell2025scaling}.

\paragraph{From diagnosis to practice.}\label{sec:selection_method}
Entity-level construction bypasses both failure mechanisms ($+1.40$\,pp Few-NERD, $+1.02$\,pp SciERC, multi-seed mean; Table~\ref{tab:entity_construction}), complementary with LP selection and governed by LP-quality alignment (\S\ref{sec:prescriptive}).
Alternative strategies (DALS, MBR, DGS) fail to reliably beat greedy (Appendix~\ref{app:dals}).
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding; settings with greater output diversity may restore selection headroom (Appendix~\ref{app:when_selection_works}).

\section{Conclusion}\label{sec:conclusion}

Five confidence signals achieve reliable NER quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.50, AUROC up to 0.82), enabling selective prediction ($+5$--$8$\,pp F1 at 80\% coverage).
Instance-level selection fails due to degeneracy and LP compression, but the diagnostic naturally motivates entity-level construction, adapting entity voting to stochastic sampling: LP-weighted aggregation yields $+1.40$\,pp on Few-NERD and $+1.02$\,pp on SciERC (multi-seed mean, $p{<}0.005$).
Construction and LP selection are complementary on two informative datasets (SciERC and Few-NERD; CoNLL operates in a ceiling regime), governed by LP-quality alignment.
For practitioners: use QE-based selective prediction when deployment requires reliability guarantees; apply entity construction when multi-sample generation is feasible; assess LP-alignment via held-out validation to choose between construction and LP selection.
As models improve, degeneracy rises and the selection window narrows; content-aware verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers} may be needed to close the remaining gap.

3	\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}

\section{Related Work}\label{sec:related}

\paragraph{Self-consistency and test-time scaling.}
Self-consistency \cite{wang2023selfconsistency} improves reasoning via majority voting; extensions handle free-form text \cite{chen2024usc, thirukovalluru2024atomic, manakul2023selfcheckgpt}.
Test-time scaling studies \cite{snell2025scaling, brown2024monkeys} and reward-free selectors \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc, kang2025selfcertainty, wang2025rankedvoting, oh2026latentsc} rely on answer-level agreement.
Adaptive variants gate on answer agreement \cite{aggarwal2023adaptive}, input difficulty \cite{wang2025make, feng2025optimal}, or response confidence \cite{kim2026reasc}; \citet{chen2025twofailures} diagnose SC failure modes without proposing gating.
All target discrete-answer reasoning; structured prediction requires different gating signals because degeneracy operates at the entity-set level.

\paragraph{Consistency for structured IE.}
\citet{yao2026consistency} show consistency correlates with accuracy for LLM-based NER/RE; we show correlation alone does not ensure selection gains, diagnosing degeneracy and compression as blocking mechanisms.
CoCoA \cite{vashurin2025cocoa} fuses confidence with consistency; our supervised baseline confirms combination is not the bottleneck (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
Earlier work on confidence for structured prediction \cite{culotta2004confidence, mejer2010confidence, fomicheva2020unsupervised} establishes the paradigm we extend to set-valued outputs.
Ensemble approaches aggregate predictions from multiple models or prompts \cite{florian2003named, xiao2025el4ner}; LLM-Blender \cite{jiang2023llmblender} fuses outputs from multiple LLMs via pairwise ranking, whereas our single-model stochastic sampling derives diversity from temperature rather than model heterogeneity.
Our entity-level construction similarly aggregates across samples from a single model, without requiring model diversity.
Our evaluation builds on generative IE \cite{zhou2024uniner, sainz2024gollie, li2023codeie, wadhwa2023revisiting, xie2024selfimproving} and constrained decoding \cite{willard2023guided, dong2024xgrammar, park2024grammar, schall2025hidden}.
\citet{yun2025price} show structured formats induce diversity collapse; our LP compression (median range 0.041 nats; \S\ref{sec:discussion}) corroborates this for NER.

\paragraph{Uncertainty estimation and MBR decoding.}
Surveys cover confidence estimation \cite{geng2024confidence}, uncertainty quantification \cite{xia2025survey}, and calibration \cite{hobelsberger2025systematic}; semantic uncertainty \cite{kuhn2023semantic, farquhar2024detecting} and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} provide model-internal alternatives.
Our selection strategies instantiate MBR decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, deguchi2024centroid}; unlike MT where MBR yields consistent gains \cite{freitag2022high} and code generation where execution-based MBR improves selection \cite{shi2022mbr}, instance degeneracy eliminates the headroom MBR needs even when utility is well-aligned ($\rho{=}0.52$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}).
\citet{eikema2025structured} find MBR utilities degrade on structured outputs; our diagnosis is complementary: degeneracy, not utility misalignment, is the primary bottleneck.
Our QE results connect to selective prediction \cite{geifman2017selective, kuleshov2015calibrated, varshney2022investigating}: signals with AUROC up to 0.82 support abstention policies independent of sample selection.

\paragraph{Best-of-$N$ with learned verifiers.}
\citet{gao2023scaling} establish BoN scaling laws and \citet{chen2021evaluating} define the pass@$k$ metric for code generation; our unsupervised signals face a more fundamental limitation than reward overoptimization.
Trained verifiers \cite{cobbe2021verifiers, lightman2024verify, fernandes2022quality} and self-evaluation guided search \cite{xie2023selfevaluation} learn per-sample scoring.
CISC \cite{taubenfeld2025cisc} and Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} derive per-sample confidence from hidden states rather than output statistics, but require architecture-specific access to intermediate representations; these hidden-state signals remain untested for structured prediction (\S Limitations).
Fine-tuning \cite{kirk2024understanding} and constrained decoding \cite{holtzman2020curious, vijayakumar2018diverse} both limit the diversity recoverable for selection.

1	Our evaluation covers four NER datasets; an exploratory RE extension on SciERC is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension} but generalization to other RE benchmarks remains unvalidated.
2	All experiments use English-language datasets; cross-lingual generalization remains untested.
3	We cover 4B\textendash 8B scale; whether the gap holds for 70B+ models or closed-source APIs is untested. Larger models may produce more diverse samples (potentially reducing degeneracy), but their LP-quality alignment behavior is unknown, and these two factors may shift in opposite directions.
4	Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.
5	
6	We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
7	The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
8	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
9	LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
10	We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
11	Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
12	The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
13	We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
14	Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
15	Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
16	Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

Our supervised approaches (DeBERTa verifier, hidden state probes, MLP/RF on signal combinations) all fail to close the oracle gap; whether content-aware verifiers with access to task-specific structure could succeed remains open.

We evaluate at $N{=}8$ (primary) and $N{=}16$; behavior at larger sample sizes is unknown (Appendix~\ref{app:n_scaling}).
The free-form ablation covers SciERC NER and CoNLL NER with one model; RE free-form results are in Appendix~\ref{app:re_extension}.
Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint used empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks; a three-part analysis rules out this confound (Appendix~\ref{app:thinking_token}).
LP compression worsens on easy datasets at lower temperature (CoNLL tied fractions reach 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$); whether reduced temperature translates to selection gains remains untested.
We tested verbalized confidence \cite{lin2022teaching, tian2023calibration} as a second per-sample signal; it exhibits severe overconfidence (mean 8.58/10 on SciERC, 9.24/10 on CoNLL) and yields the weakest QE and selection among all signals (Appendix~\ref{app:verbalized_confidence}).
Ad-hoc LP${\times}$VC combinations yield at most $+0.2$~pp over greedy (not significant; \S\ref{sec:discussion}); whether \textit{learned} combinations could close the gap remains open.
The $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold used for tied/non-tied LP stratification is a post-hoc exploratory choice; while selection F1 is stable across $\varepsilon \in [0, 0.2]$ (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), the specific subset gains should be interpreted as characterizing the compression phenomenon rather than as a tuned selection strategy.
We tested one remedy for LP compression (entity-token-only LP, excluding format/schema tokens) which fails to improve selection despite increasing within-instance variance on SciERC ($4{\times}$); LP${\times}$VC combinations also fail to recover selection (\S\ref{sec:discussion}). Our supervised signal combination baseline uses only the five unsupervised signals studied; a DeBERTa verifier encoding input-output pairs also fails to close the gap (preliminary, SciERC $n{=}106$), hidden state probes on the generating model's representations improve correlation ($+37$\% on SciERC) but do not improve selection (gap closure $-5.1$\%; Appendix~\ref{app:hidden_probe}), ; the bottleneck extends to model-internal access. Entity embeddings and calibration-based approaches remain untested.
Other per-sample scoring methods exist but were not evaluated: Self-Certainty \cite{kang2025selfcertainty} (consistency of token-level self-evaluation) and P(True) \cite{kadavath2022language} (model's own probability estimate of correctness) both produce per-sample scores and could in principle address the alignment bottleneck; whether they suffer from similar compression under fine-tuning is unknown.
Our selection experiments use 3 training seeds for Few-NERD and CoNLL (stability $\sigma{\leq}0.04$~pp for LP selection); these confirm robustness on the key positive and negative datasets. SciERC uses 1 primary seed with high seed sensitivity ($\sigma{=}0.48$~pp, $n{=}529$), which reflects limited within-seed statistical power.
Few-NERD models are trained for 3 epochs (vs.\ 5 for other datasets) due to earlier convergence; epoch confound analyses on both Few-NERD (2-point) and SciERC (3-point, including 10-epoch overfitting) are provided in Appendix~\ref{app:epoch_confound}.

165	\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
166	Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
167	Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
168	Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$; the two selection rules are equivalent.
169	Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
170	Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
171	Evaluation circularity is negligible.

253	\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
254	Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
255	For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
256	Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
257	This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
258	For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
259	The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.
260	
261	\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
262	While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
263	VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
264	These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
265	This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

369	\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
370	The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
371	Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
372	The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
373	These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
374	We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
375	The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.

377	On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
378	The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

400	\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
401	The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
402	To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
403	(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
404	(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
405	(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.
406	
407	Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
408	On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
409	On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
410	On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
411	These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.
412	
413	\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
414	Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
415	Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
416	The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over the 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$). However, the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory.
417	For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.
418	
419	\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}\label{app:when_selection_works}
420	Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
421	(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
422	(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
423	(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
424	(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

428	\subsection{Supervised Signal Combination}
429	
430	Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
431	Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
432	To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
433	DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).

\section{Robustness Analysis}\label{app:robustness}

We exclude instances with empty gold annotations from all correlation analyses (CoNLL: 697/3{,}453 instances, 20.2\%; SciERC: 22/551, 4.0\%).
For these instances, F1 is trivially zero regardless of prediction quality, and consistency signals reflect agreement on the empty set rather than extraction quality. Including them inflates or deflates Spearman $\rho$ depending on signal behavior at the boundary.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_temperature_robustness}
\caption{Temperature robustness on SciERC ($N{=}8$). Top: NER; bottom: RE. SJ maintains stable $\rho$ across $T{=}0.7$ and $T{=}1.0$, while FK shows mixed sensitivity. LP shows the largest NER temperature effect ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.044$); RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data unavailable.}
\label{fig:temperature_robustness}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Temperature sensitivity.}
SJ NER $\rho$ shifts from 0.364 ($T{=}0.7$) to 0.360 ($T{=}1.0$), a difference of 0.004.
FK NER $\rho$ drops by 0.022, while RE $\rho$ increases by 0.091, likely reflecting reduced diversity at lower temperature interacting differently across tasks.
LP exhibits the largest temperature effect on NER ($\rho{=}0.249$ at $T{=}0.7$ vs.\ $0.205$ at $T{=}1.0$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.044$), consistent with lower temperature concentrating probability mass and improving LP's discriminative power for quality estimation; RE $T{=}0.7$ LP data is not available.
Across all comparisons, the signal hierarchy is preserved at both temperatures on NER (SJ${>}$FK${>}$LP at $T{=}0.7$: $0.364{>}0.289{>}0.249$; at $T{=}1.0$: $0.360{>}0.267{>}0.205$).

\paragraph{Sample size scaling.}
Increasing from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$ improves SJ on Qwen SciERC NER: $\rho$ rises from 0.360 to $0.411{\pm}0.010$ (three seeds: 0.398, 0.423, 0.410), a gain of $+0.047$.
The magnitude of $N$-scaling gains is setting-dependent (LLaMA SciERC NER yields $+0.016$ and Qwen CoNLL NER $+0.014$), though the direction is consistently positive.
LLaMA CoNLL exhibits the most uniform scaling: all four consistency signals gain $\Delta\rho{\approx}{+}0.042$ (range: $+0.039$ to $+0.044$) while LP gains only $+0.004$ (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
FK $N$-scaling is seed-dependent: Qwen SciERC gains range from $+0.005$ to $+0.023$ across seeds (mean $+0.016$), while LLaMA CoNLL yields $+0.039$ (3-seed mean); individual seed FK shifts vary substantially under the unified pipeline, so this should not be interpreted as a robust trend.
VC $N$-scaling is consistently positive ($+0.005$ on Qwen CoNLL, $+0.018$ on LLaMA SciERC, $+0.030$ on Qwen SciERC), while LP is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta{\leq}0.034$).
SJ, EM, and VC scale consistently across all tested settings; only FK shows seed-dependent variation that does not constitute a reliable trend, structural and binary-agreement signals are the most robust to $N$.
At $N{=}16$, SJ converges to comparable NER performance with VC ($\Delta{=}0.002$) while exhibiting lower cross-seed variance ($\sigma{=}0.010$ vs.\ $0.026$), a more stable alternative at higher sample sizes.

\paragraph{Transfer across model families.}
LLaMA-3.1-8B-Instruct shows a similar SJ--FK ordering on SciERC NER (SJ $\rho{=}0.325{\pm}0.021$, FK $\rho{=}0.256{\pm}0.024$, $\Delta\rho{=}0.069$; permutation $p{=}0.06$, borderline).
On CoNLL, the gap across model families is minimal (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): SJ achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ (LLaMA) vs.\ 0.436 (Qwen), $\Delta{=}0.005$.
At $N{=}16$, the structural-over-LP advantage holds across all four tested NER settings: Qwen SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.409$ vs.\ LP 0.239, $\Delta{=}{+}0.170$), Qwen CoNLL (EM $\rho{=}0.463$ vs.\ LP 0.328, $\Delta{=}{+}0.135$),\footnote{Qwen CoNLL $N{=}16$ was not recomputed under the unified pipeline; LP $\rho{=}0.328$ may differ slightly from the registry value (0.315) due to instance filtering.} LLaMA SciERC (VC $\rho{=}0.452$ vs.\ LP 0.277, $\Delta{=}{+}0.175$), and LLaMA CoNLL 3-seed (SJ $\rho{=}0.474{\pm}0.009$ vs.\ LP $0.311{\pm}0.003$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.163$).

\paragraph{FK independence: instance-level permutation test.}\label{app:fk_independence}

To verify that Fleiss' $\kappa$ reflects genuine within-instance agreement rather than marginal-rate artifacts, we conduct instance-level permutation tests across three configurations.
For each instance, we permute sample labels 10{,}000 times to generate a null distribution of FK under independence, then compare the observed FK against this null via a one-sample $t$-test and permutation $p$-value.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Instance-level FK independence test. Permutation tests confirm FK reflects true within-instance agreement (all $p{<}0.001$). Split-half reliability $r$ computed by randomly partitioning $N$ samples into two halves and correlating their FK scores.}
\label{tab:fk_independence}
\begin{tabular}{lrcccc}
\toprule
Config & $n$ & FK mean & 95\% CI & $t$ & Split-half $r$ \\
\midrule
SciERC (Qwen) & 529 & 0.402 & [0.376, 0.428] & 30.8 & 0.395 \\
CoNLL (LLaMA) & 2{,}756 & 0.927 & [0.919, 0.935] & 225.9 & 0.578 \\
CoNLL (Qwen) & 2{,}756 & 0.720 & [0.706, 0.734] & 102.1 & 0.520 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:fk_independence} reports the results.
All configurations reject the independence null at $p{<}0.001$ ($n{=}529$--$2{,}756$), FK captures genuine inter-sample agreement rather than chance label co-occurrence.
Split-half reliability ranges from $r{=}0.395$ (SciERC) to $r{=}0.578$ (CoNLL LLaMA), moderate stability: FK estimates from half the samples correlate positively with those from the other half, though the SciERC value suggests noisier estimation on harder tasks with fewer samples.
The higher FK means on CoNLL ($0.720$--$0.927$) vs.\ SciERC ($0.402$) mirror the difficulty gradient observed in the main quality estimation results.

\section{Additional Analyses}\label{app:additional}

\begin{figure*}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\textwidth]{fig_signal_heatmap}
\caption{Quality estimation heatmap (Spearman $\rho$) across five signals and four configurations. Left: full evaluation set; right: conditional set (non-zero F1 instances). On the full set, structural signals dominate on SciERC NER while all signals converge on CoNLL. On the conditional set, EM emerges as the strongest signal on both NER ($\rho{=}0.360$) and RE ($\rho{=}0.417$), while LP RE collapses to near-zero ($\rho{=}0.011$).}
\label{fig:signal_heatmap}
\end{figure*}

\paragraph{Per-relation diagnostic.}
RE signal degradation is relation-specific.
\textsc{Feature-Of} has near-zero correlation ($\rho{=}0.004$), while \textsc{Hyponym-Of} achieves $\rho{=}0.646$.
The primary bottleneck is entity span errors, which account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives. This is a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect, as they measure agreement among equally incorrect extractions.
We note that RE analysis relies on a single dataset (SciERC); generalization to other RE benchmarks remains to be validated.

\paragraph{Capability stratification.}
For NER, SJ effectiveness scales with structural complexity: on SciERC instances with 6+ entities, $\rho{=}0.547$, compared to $\rho{=}0.415$ for 1--2 entities.
The SJ advantage over LP remains stable across sentence-length quartiles ($\Delta\rho{\approx}0.08$--$0.20$).
For RE, SJ $\rho$ increases monotonically with sentence length (Q1: 0.110 $\to$ Q4: 0.473; Fisher $z$-test $p{=}0.004$): longer, more relation-dense sentences provide richer structure for consistency-based estimation.
Both proxies are weakly correlated with F1 ($|r|{<}0.15$), they capture input complexity rather than directly predicting output quality; however, entity count and sentence length are themselves moderately correlated ($\rho{=}0.650$), so they reflect overlapping rather than independent complexity dimensions.
For RE, entity count and relation count are strongly correlated ($\rho{=}0.769$) and thus reflect a single structural complexity dimension rather than independent axes.
On the high-complexity RE subset ($n{=}81$, high relation count), signals improve substantially: VC reaches $\rho{=}0.630$, LP $\rho{=}0.554$, and SJ $\rho{=}0.502$, all far above the full-set levels.
Richer relational structure provides more signal for consistency-based estimation, complementing the task-level boundary established by WNUT-17: structural signals are most effective within a ``sweet spot'' of sufficient model capability and sufficient output complexity.

\paragraph{Length vs.\ log-probability.}
Figure~\ref{fig:length_logprob_scatter} shows that mean log-probability is weakly positively correlated with output length (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$, $n{=}4{,}232$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$, $n{=}3{,}176$), ruling out length-penalty confounding as an explanation for LP's selection failure: longer outputs receive \textit{higher}, not lower, token-averaged log-probability under constrained decoding.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{fig_length_logprob_scatter}
\caption{Output length vs.\ mean log-probability on SciERC ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$). Positive correlations (NER: $\rho{=}0.386$; RE: $\rho{=}0.326$) rule out length-penalty confounding.}
\label{fig:length_logprob_scatter}
\end{figure}

\paragraph{Evaluation circularity and LOO-SJ equivalence.}
Consensus-proximity selection chooses $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Leave-one-out SJ (LOO-SJ) for sample $y_i$ is $\text{LOO-SJ}_i = \frac{1}{N-1}\sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$.
Since the $\frac{1}{N-1}$ constant is shared across all candidates within an instance, $\arg\max_{y_i} \text{LOO-SJ}_i = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} \text{SJ}(y_i, y_j)$; the two selection rules are equivalent.
Standard (non-LOO) SJ adds the self-comparison term $\text{SJ}(y_i, y_i) = 1$ to each candidate, which is constant and thus does not affect ranking.
Empirically, LOO-SJ yields $\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.014$ relative to standard SJ (a correlation-level difference), with a maximum per-instance score difference of $3.1{\times}10^{-4}$ (negligible at the individual prediction level).
Evaluation circularity is negligible.

\paragraph{SJ normalizer robustness.}
Equation~\ref{eq:sj} uses $\max(|g_i|, |g_j|)$ as the denominator; an alternative is the union size $|g_i \cup g_j|$.
Table~\ref{tab:sj_normalizer} compares the two normalizers across all six model--dataset combinations ($N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, seed${=}42$): $|\Delta\rho|{<}0.01$ in every case, the choice between max and union normalization does not affect conclusions.

\centering
\small

\paragraph{Conditional filtering details.}
On LLaMA conditional RE (non-zero F1 instances), SJ recovers to $\rho{=}0.405$ while FK drops to $\rho{=}0.259$, consistent with the NER structural advantage; on full-set RE, however, the SJ--FK difference is non-significant ($\Delta\rho{=}{-}0.005$, $p{=}0.53$; preliminary).
At $N{=}16$, the divergence persists: SJ maintains $\rho{=}0.308$ on conditional RE while LP drops to $\rho{=}{-}0.026$.
EM ranks first across all four tested conditional configurations: SciERC NER ($\rho{=}0.360$), CoNLL Qwen $N{=}16$ ($\rho{=}0.466$), CoNLL LLaMA 3-seed ($\rho{=}0.462$), and SciERC RE ($\rho{=}0.417$). This holds despite full-set rankings ranging from \#1 (CoNLL Qwen) to \#5 (SciERC RE).
On the full set, EM is diluted by trivial agreement: instances where all $N$ samples produce identical (possibly incorrect) outputs receive EM${=}1$ regardless of quality, compressing the signal's dynamic range.
On the conditional set, where the model demonstrably produces varied outputs, exact agreement becomes the strongest quality signal.
The margin over SJ is largest on RE ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.171$), where compound extraction decisions amplify output variability, and smallest on CoNLL LLaMA ($\Delta\rho{=}{+}0.002$), where all signals converge near $\rho{\approx}0.46$.

\paragraph{WNUT-17 full signal analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:wnut} reports all five signals on WNUT-17 with full-set and conditional $\rho$.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Quality estimation on WNUT-17 (Qwen, $N{=}16$, $T{=}1.0$, $n{=}689$). Cond: non-zero F1 instances ($n{=}334$). Full-set $\rho$ reflects binary success prediction; conditional $\rho$ measures quality gradation. LP's conditional $\rho$ is highest despite negative full-set $\rho$.}
\label{tab:wnut}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Signal & $\rho$ & AUROC & Cond.\ $\rho$ & Cond.\ $p$ \\
\midrule
VC      & .724 & .913 & .038 & .487 \\
FK      & .125 & .555 & .169 & .002 \\
SJ      & .089 & .517 & .288 & ${<}$1e-7 \\
EM      & .050 & .487 & .333 & ${<}$1e-9 \\
LP & $-$.410 & .219 & .350 & ${<}$1e-10 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}
The full-set $p$-values are: VC ${<}$1e-112, FK $p{=}0.001$, SJ $p{=}0.020$, EM $p{=}0.194$, LP ${<}$1e-28.
VC's high full-set $\rho{=}0.724$ is entirely driven by the zero/non-zero boundary (conditional $\rho{=}0.038$, $p{=}0.49$), while LP's conditional $\rho{=}0.350$ is the highest among all signals on the non-zero subset, full-set correlations on high-failure-rate datasets conflate binary success prediction with quality gradation.

\paragraph{Cross-configuration selection analysis.}
Table~\ref{tab:cross_selection} extends the selection analysis to five additional configurations.
On LLaMA SciERC, where output diversity remains substantial (18\% identical outputs, 39\% unique), LP achieves the highest selection F1 (0.652) at $N{=}8$ but still falls within bootstrap noise of single-sample (0.646), replicating the gap observed on Qwen SciERC (Table~\ref{tab:selection}).
On LLaMA FewNERD ($n{=}32{,}565$, 3-seed mean), LP is the only signal with positive selection ($+0.36$~pp), confirming LP as the most robust selection signal across model families (Qwen FewNERD: $+1.39$~pp, Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}). All structural signals degrade selection (VC $-2.39$~pp, SJ $-0.52$~pp), consistent with the Qwen pattern. LLaMA FewNERD degeneracy ($23.4{\pm}4.7$\%, 3 seeds) is higher than Qwen ($12.7$\%), illustrating the capability-diversity tension: LLaMA achieves stronger greedy F1 ($0.784$ vs.\ $0.748$, $+3.6$~pp) but at the cost of higher degeneracy ($+10.7$~pp) and reduced oracle headroom ($10.0$ vs.\ $12.4$~pp).
On CoNLL, 48--87\% of instances produce identical outputs across all $N$ samples; this reflects a ceiling effect (single-sample F1 ${\approx}$0.91--0.92) rather than signal failure, and selection analysis on these configurations is uninformative because there is little per-sample variance for any signal to exploit.

\begin{table*}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Best-of-$N$ selection F1 (macro, instance-averaged) across configurations ($T{=}1.0$, 3-seed mean). Best non-oracle signal per row in \textbf{bold}. LP is the only signal with positive selection on both FewNERD configurations (Qwen $+1.39$~pp, Table~\ref{tab:fewnerd}; LLaMA $+0.36$~pp). At $N{=}16$ on LLaMA CoNLL, VC achieves small but significant gains ($+0.28$~pp, $p{<}0.03$; see text below). CoNLL shows especially tight clustering where greedy already exceeds 0.90.}
\label{tab:cross_selection}
\begin{tabular}{llccccccc}
\toprule

\paragraph{Diminishing returns of $N$-scaling.}
Our $N{=}8$ and $N{=}16$ comparisons (Table~\ref{tab:robustness}) characterize the marginal value of additional samples for test-time scaling \cite{brown2024monkeys, snell2025scaling}.
For quality estimation, structural signals benefit consistently but sublinearly: SJ $\rho$ improves by $+0.047$ (Qwen SciERC, 3-seed mean) and $+0.032$ (LLaMA CoNLL, 3-seed mean) when doubling from $N{=}8$ to $N{=}16$, while log-probability is approximately $N$-invariant ($\Delta\rho{\leq}0.021$).
Structural signals use $\binom{N}{2}$ pairwise comparisons (28 pairs at $N{=}8$, 120 at $N{=}16$), but the $\rho$ improvement is far less than proportional, each additional comparison yields diminishing information.
This asymmetry gives structural signals a relative advantage in the compute-constrained regime: at $N{=}8$, SJ already achieves $\rho{=}0.431$ on LLaMA CoNLL (vs.\ LP $\rho{=}0.307$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.124$), and the gap \textit{widens} at $N{=}16$ ($\Delta{=}{+}0.163$) because structural signals continue to benefit from additional pairwise evidence while LP does not.
For sample selection, additional samples increase the oracle upper bound (more draws raise the probability of a high-quality candidate), but signal-based selection remains flat because the selector's inability to identify the best candidate is a granularity limitation, not a sample size limitation.
The practical implication is that $N{=}8$ captures most of the achievable quality estimation benefit; further scaling widens rather than closes the correlation-selection gap absent stronger per-sample selectors.

\paragraph{$N{=}16$ CoNLL selection: small but significant.}
While quality estimation benefits sublinearly from $N$-scaling, selection behavior at $N{=}16$ reveals a nuanced exception on LLaMA CoNLL.
VC achieves the largest gain over single-sample ($+0.28$~pp, $p{=}0.003$--$0.027$ across 3 seeds, all significant), with SJ, FK, and EM at $+0.22$--$0.23$~pp and LP at $+0.12$~pp (2/3 seeds significant).
These gains are statistically significant but practically minimal: oracle headroom at $N{=}16$ is only 2.5~pp, so VC captures approximately 10\% of the available headroom.
This reinforces the primary finding: even under the most favorable conditions (high baseline performance, more candidates, and aggregated multi-seed evidence), signal-based selection recovers only a fraction of the oracle headroom available.

On the 44\% of Qwen SciERC instances with high diversity (${\geq}4$ unique outputs among 8 samples, $n{=}232$), oracle headroom reaches $+$16.3~pp, yet all consistency-based signals (SJ, FK, EM, VC) select at or below single-sample, and LP, the only per-sample signal, achieves merely $+$0.8~pp.
