\paragraph{TOST equivalence testing.}\label{app:tost}
The primary evidence against selection gains comes from effect sizes and confidence intervals: Cohen's $d{=}0.038$ for the best signal (NER LP) and bootstrap 95\% CI [$-$3.0, $+$4.2]~pp spanning zero.
Table~\ref{tab:tost} supplements this with two one-sided tests (TOST), testing whether each signal's selection F1 is equivalent to single-sample within a bound $\delta$.
The $\delta$ values are contextualized against oracle headroom (12--18~pp): $\delta{=}5$~pp corresponds to forgoing 28--38\% of the available headroom, $\delta{=}3$~pp forgoing 17--23\%, and $\delta{=}2$~pp less than 15\%.
These proportions use the same test data that defines the headroom, introducing circularity: $\delta$ is anchored to the very quantity it contextualizes.
We address this below with externally anchored equivalence margins.
The breakpoint $\delta^*$, the minimum equivalence margin at which each signal passes TOST, ranges from approximately 1.3~pp (SJ, ${\sim}$10\% of oracle headroom) to 3.4~pp (FK, ${\sim}$26\%) on NER, and from approximately 2.9~pp (LP, ${\sim}$16\%) to 6.5~pp (VC, ${\sim}$36\%) on RE.
On NER ($n{=}529$), at $\delta{=}{\pm}2$~pp, SJ and LP are confirmed equivalent to single-sample (TOST $p{<}0.05$); at $\delta{=}{\pm}3$~pp, four of five signals pass; at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp, all five pass.
On RE ($n{=}397$, preliminary), EM and VC fail equivalence even at $\delta{=}{\pm}5$~pp due to systematic underperformance ($\Delta{=}{-}3.2$~pp and $-4.5$~pp respectively).
The effect sizes are negligible ($d{=}0.038$) and confidence intervals span zero, with TOST confirming equivalence at practically meaningful margins.

\paragraph{External equivalence margins.}
The oracle-headroom anchors above introduce circularity: $\delta$ is calibrated against the very quantity it contextualizes.
To resolve this, we supplement with three externally grounded margins:
(1) $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}$: the bootstrapped standard error of single-sample F1 (0.43--1.33~pp depending on configuration), which represents measurement noise;
(2) $\delta_{\mathrm{practical}}{=}0.5$~pp, the threshold below which NER differences are considered negligible \cite{ratinov2009design};
(3) $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}{=}1.0$~pp, the approximate significant-difference threshold established in NER evaluation methodology \cite{bergkirkpatrick2012empirical}.

Results under these external anchors diverge sharply by configuration.
On LLaMA CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), all signals pass equivalence at every $\delta$ ($p{<}0.001$), consistent with the near-zero selection deltas ($|\Delta|{\leq}0.1$~pp) and tight CIs at this sample size.
On Qwen CoNLL ($n{=}2{,}756$), no signal passes at any external $\delta$: selection F1 degrades by 0.9--1.5~pp relative to single-sample, which exceeds even $\delta_{\mathrm{literature}}$.
On SciERC NER ($n{=}529$), only SJ passes at $\delta_{\mathrm{SEM}}{=}1.33$~pp (the widest SEM bound); all other signals and tighter margins fail.
These external anchors confirm that the equivalence conclusion is configuration-dependent: LLaMA CoNLL selection is robustly equivalent to single-sample under any reasonable margin, while SciERC and Qwen CoNLL selection shows detectable degradation at externally calibrated thresholds.

\paragraph{Multiple comparison considerations.}\label{app:multiple_comparisons}
Our primary selection analysis involves ${\sim}$20 comparisons (5 signals $\times$ 3--4 configurations).
Since all primary selection results are non-significant ($p{>}0.05$), applying Benjamini-Hochberg correction can only make these results more conservative, strengthening the ``no signal beats greedy'' conclusion.
The sole positive finding, the non-tied LP subset ($+2.9$~pp, $p{=}0.004$; \S\ref{sec:discussion}), survives Bonferroni correction over the 5 signal comparisons ($p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.020 < 0.05$). However, the $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ threshold is selected post-hoc from a 7-point sweep (Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}); joint correction across thresholds and signals yields $p_{\mathrm{adj}}{=}0.14$, so this finding is exploratory.
For quality estimation signal rankings, differences between the top signals (e.g., VC vs.\ SJ on SciERC) should be interpreted as descriptive rather than as statistically confirmed orderings, given the limited power of 3-seed comparisons.

\paragraph{When would consistency-based selection work?}\label{app:when_selection_works}
Our negative results are specific to fine-tuned models with constrained decoding on structured IE. Several conditions outside our experimental scope could restore selection headroom.
(a)~Models with poor calibration or in-context learning setups (without fine-tuning) produce more diverse outputs, widening the gap between candidates that consistency signals can exploit.
(b)~Closed-source APIs where log-probabilities are unavailable make consistency signals the only viable selection mechanism; our structural signals (SJ, VC, FK, EM) provide quality estimation ($\rho$ up to 0.45) even without model-internal access.
(c)~Ensemble or mixture-of-experts settings generate structurally diverse candidates by design, reducing instance degeneracy below the levels observed in our single-model sampling.
(d)~Tasks where the model exhibits systematic overconfidence (e.g., hallucination-prone generation) may benefit from consensus filtering, as disagreement among samples would carry more discriminative signal than in our well-calibrated fine-tuned regime.

\section{Supervised and Model-Internal Signal Analysis}\label{app:supervised_combination}

\subsection{Supervised Signal Combination}

Supervised classifiers (logistic regression, MLP, random forest) trained on all five signals (5-fold CV, 3-seed mean, SciERC, $N{=}16$, $+17.9$~pp headroom) all perform at or below greedy (F1${=}0.644$; LR: $-0.4$~pp; MLP: $-1.6$~pp; RF: $-3.1$~pp).
Adding pairwise interaction features does not help (AUROC 0.634 vs.\ 0.638).
To test whether richer representations could close the gap, we train a DeBERTa-v3-base verifier that encodes input-output pairs and predicts per-sample F1.
DeBERTa achieves $\rho{=}0.329{\pm}0.087$ (5-fold CV, 3 seeds). Despite moderate quality prediction, selection utility is poor: on SciERC, DeBERTa closes $-26.5{\pm}26.5$\% of the oracle gap (13 of 15 runs negative; vs.\ LP's $+4.2{\pm}10.7$\%); on Few-NERD, DeBERTa recovers only $+3.5$\% (single 80/20 split; vs.\ LP's $+16.3$\%).
Cross-dataset transfer fails entirely ($-27$\% to $-72$\% gap closure).
Neither handcrafted signal combinations nor learned text representations close the selection gap; only model-internal log-probability provides meaningful selection signal, consistent with an information asymmetry between the generating model and external observers.

\subsection{Hidden State Probes}\label{app:hidden_probe}

The preceding negative results suggest the bottleneck is model-internal rather than a feature engineering problem.
We test this directly by training probes on the generating model's hidden representations.

\paragraph{Setup.}
For each of $N{=}8$ samples per instance, we extract the mean-pooled final-layer hidden state ($d{=}4096$) from the generating Qwen3-8B model and train a linear probe and a two-layer MLP (hidden dim${=}256$) to predict per-sample F1 (5-fold CV, 3 seeds).

A learned token-level LP aggregator (1D CNN over per-token log-probabilities) matches mean LP on Few-NERD (gap closure $56.4$\% vs.\ $55.8$\%); LP's bottleneck is not token aggregation.
The correlation-selection gap extends to model-internal representations: in the high-capability regime (greedy F1${=}0.644$), inter-sample F1 differences are small enough that improved ranking provides no marginal selection value, consistent with the capability-diversity tension (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

554	\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}
555	
556	Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
557	We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.
558	
559	\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
560	Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
561	The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
562	Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.
563	
564	\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
565	All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
566	Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.
567	
568	\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
569	CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
570	If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
571	Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

826	\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}
827	
828	\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
829	Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
830	Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
831	\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.
832	
833	\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
834	The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
835	On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
836	The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
837	This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
838	This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
839	The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
840	Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
841	Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

\paragraph{Prompt template.}
For NER, we use a structured prompt:
\begin{quote}
\small
\texttt{System:} You are an expert in Named Entity Recognition.\\
\texttt{User:} Extract all named entities from the following text. Output as JSON.\\
Text: \texttt{\{input\_text\}}\\
Entity types: \texttt{\{schema\_types\}}
\end{quote}
RE follows the same structure with ``Relation Extraction'' and relation type lists substituted accordingly.

\paragraph{Constrained decoding.}
Inference uses vLLM with XGrammar-based JSON schema enforcement \cite{dong2024xgrammar, willard2023guided}, which constrains outputs to valid entity/relation structures matching the target schema.
This eliminates format errors but may compress per-sample diversity by restricting the output space.\footnote{SciERC training used \texttt{enable\_thinking=True} (LLaMA Factory 0.9.4 default), injecting empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks (4--5 tokens) into each training response with loss computation; CoNLL and WNUT explicitly set \texttt{enable\_thinking=False}. Constrained decoding at inference time enforces JSON-only output, suppressing thinking tokens. See \S\ref{sec:setup} and Limitations for discussion of this confound.}

\section{Thinking Token Impact Analysis}\label{app:thinking_token}

Qwen3-8B's SciERC checkpoint was trained with empty \texttt{<think></think>} blocks prepended to each response (\S\ref{sec:setup}).
We quantify the potential impact on LP scores through three complementary arguments.

\paragraph{LP shift magnitude.}
Empty thinking tokens (mean 4.5 per sample) constitute 2.1\% of tokens on SciERC.
The estimated LP shift is 0.001 nats per token (2.68\% of the median within-instance LP range of 0.041 nats).
Because all samples share identical thinking-token LP offsets, cumulative LP rankings are invariant; mean LP changes selection for ${<}1.5\%$ of instances.

\paragraph{Constant prefix cancellation.}
All $N$ samples within an instance share the same prompt and, under constrained decoding, the same absence of thinking tokens at inference time.
Any LP bias from the training-time thinking prefix is therefore a near-constant additive shift across all candidates within an instance, leaving within-instance LP \textit{rankings} unchanged.

\paragraph{CoNLL control group.}
CoNLL and WNUT-17 checkpoints were trained without thinking tokens (\texttt{enable\_thinking=False}).
If thinking tokens caused LP compression on SciERC, CoNLL should exhibit lower tied fractions.
Instead, CoNLL shows \textit{higher} tied fractions at both temperatures (86.8\% at $T{=}1.0$, 95.8\% at $T{=}0.7$) than SciERC (60.3\% at $T{=}1.0$), directly contradicting the thinking-token hypothesis.

\section{Log-Probability Score Compression}\label{app:logprob_ties}

Under constrained decoding, log-probability scores are severely compressed within instances, limiting per-sample discrimination (Table~\ref{tab:logprob_ties}, Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}).
The median within-instance LP range is only 0.041 nats; we use $\varepsilon{=}0.05$ as an illustrative threshold to characterize this compression.
At this cutpoint, 60.3\% of instances ($n{=}529$, excluding empty gold annotations) have a within-sample range below $\varepsilon$, and 75\% of pairwise comparisons are effective ties ($|\Delta|{<}0.026$).
The CDF rises smoothly with no cliff or discontinuity (Figure~\ref{fig:lp_range_cdf}); compression is a pervasive regime rather than a bimodal split.
This compression is stable across seeds: seed${=}456$ yields median LP range${=}0.040$ nats and tied fraction${=}62.2\%$ (vs.\ seed${=}42$: $0.041$ nats, $60.3\%$).
Seed~456 uses a different subtask flag (joint vs.\ ner for seeds 42 and 123); the LP distributions are statistically indistinguishable (median LP: 8.37 vs.\ 8.20 nats; Mann--Whitney $p{=}0.55$); the subtask change does not affect compression.
For comparison, SJ has only 12.5\% tied instances at the same threshold; SJ's advantage over LP for selection is one of score resolution, not information content.

The NER pattern reveals two complementary failure modes rather than a monotonic relationship between consistency and selection gain:
\begin{itemize}
\item \textbf{Q4 ceiling effect.} High-consistency instances (mean VC${=}0.92$) have oracle headroom of only 4.78~pp. Samples have already converged, leaving little room for any signal to improve selection.

\section{Exploratory Extension to Relation Extraction}\label{app:re_extension}

We extend the NER evaluation to relation extraction (RE) on SciERC as an exploratory single-benchmark analysis.
RE produces sets of (head, relation, tail) triples with partial overlap; 40\% of RE instances receive zero F1, and entity span errors account for 55.5\% of RE false negatives, a prerequisite failure that consistency signals cannot detect (\S\ref{app:additional}).
All RE results use Qwen3-8B unless noted; single-seed ($\text{seed}{=}42$) for $N{=}8$ analyses, 3-seed for $N{=}16$.

\paragraph{Quality estimation.}
RE quality estimation is reported in Table~\ref{tab:multiseed} (3-seed means).
The signal ranking differs from NER: VC leads ($\rho{=}0.309{\pm}0.024$), but LP rises to \#2 ($\rho{=}0.297{\pm}0.022$), above FK, SJ, and EM, a reversal reflecting RE's higher sensitivity to per-sample scoring.
RE miscalibration is more severe than NER (ECE 0.109--0.339; Figure~\ref{fig:reliability}).

\paragraph{Selection.}
Table~\ref{tab:re_cond_selection} presents RE selection at $N{=}8$: no signal outperforms single-sample (0.404) on the full set ($n{=}397$) or the non-zero subset ($n{=}238$), with 18.1~pp of unrealized oracle headroom.
At $N{=}16$ (Qwen3-4B, Table~\ref{tab:re_n16_selection}), LP is the sole positive signal ($\Delta{=}{+}0.7$~pp, $p{=}0.058$), consistent with LP being the strongest RE selection signal across scales.

\paragraph{Scale ablation.}
At 4B scale (Qwen3-4B, $N{=}8$, $\text{seed}{=}42$), RE quality estimation shows FK $\rho{=}0.359$ and LP $\rho{=}0.351$, both above their 8B counterparts (FK 0.275, LP 0.266), while SJ declines ($0.267$ vs.\ $0.250$).
Selection remains below single-sample on RE ($\Delta$ up to $-3.4$~pp) despite 17.1~pp of oracle headroom.

\paragraph{Free-form decoding.}
RE LP selection consistently reverses direction under free-form decoding ($+1.8{\pm}0.1$~pp across 4 seeds vs.\ $-0.9$~pp under constrained decoding at 8B; \S\ref{app:freeform_ablation}); constrained decoding's fixed template likely obscures LP signal in RE (\S\ref{app:mbr_discussion}).

\section{MBR Decoding and Task-Specific Interactions}\label{app:mbr_discussion}

\paragraph{Connection to MBR decoding.}
Our selection strategies instantiate minimum Bayes risk (MBR) decoding \cite{eikema2022sampling, muller2021understanding}: each selects $\hat{y} = \arg\max_{y_i} \sum_{j \neq i} U(y_i, y_j)$ with utility $U$ defined by SJ, EM, or entity overlap.
Despite MBR's success in machine translation \cite{freitag2022high} and its extension to summarization, code generation, and captioning \cite{jinnai2024mbr}, all variants fail here: despite positive within-instance utility--F1 correlation, selection gains are limited by instance degeneracy, the core of the correlation-selection gap.
\citet{eikema2025structured} study structure-conditional MBR decoding and find that standard utility functions degrade on structured outputs, consistent with our finding that consensus-proximity selection fails in IE despite its success in machine translation.

\paragraph{Task-specific decoding interactions.}
The free-form ablation reveals divergent behavior across tasks.
On RE, LP selection flips from $-0.68$~pp (constrained) to $+1.69$~pp (free-form; preliminary, single RE benchmark), a reversal that spans all 7 relation types and is driven by selective variance reallocation ($p{<}0.0001$).
The win/loss ratio shifts from 36:59 (constrained) to 45:45 (free-form), with the gains concentrated on relation-dense instances (mean 3.3 gold relations).
This interaction does not generalize to NER, where selection remains negligible under both regimes.
This ablation uses a single seed (seed${=}42$); whether the RE reversal replicates across seeds and generalizes to other RE benchmarks warrants further investigation.
The non-tied subset ($n{=}210$) is partially reshuffled under free-form decoding: Jaccard similarity between the constrained and free-form non-tied sets is 0.472: 87 instances newly gain LP discrimination while others lose it, and the newly non-tied subset shows a $3{\times}$ increase in within-instance LP range for the newly non-tied subset.
Despite this reshuffling, aggregate NER selection gains remain negligible. Score compression is not a fixed property of specific instances but rather a pervasive regime that shifts across instances without producing net selection improvement.
Free-form decoding also slightly improves quality estimation (NER VC $\rho$: 0.379$\to$0.409), though this does not translate to selection gains.

Free-form decoding removes grammar constraints entirely; outputs are parsed post-hoc (parse rate 99.95\%, 4406/4408).
LP score distributions are nearly identical across regimes (Panel~A: within-instance std ratio $0.97{\times}$), and NER selection gains remain negligible under both regimes (Panel~B).
RE LP selection consistently reverses direction under free-form decoding across 4 seeds: $+1.84{\pm}0.12$~pp (seeds 42/123/456/789: $+1.69$, $+1.76$, $+2.00$, $+1.91$~pp) vs.\ $-0.68$~pp constrained.
The constrained reference ($-0.68$~pp) uses the ablation-matched baseline; the primary experiment (Table~\ref{tab:selection}) yields $-0.9$~pp on the same gold-filtered set.
Quality estimation improves modestly for most signals under free-form decoding (Panel~C), with the largest gain for FK ($+0.053$ NER, $+0.039$ RE).

Quality estimation under free-form decoding yields SJ $\rho{=}0.461$, EM $\rho{=}0.471$, LP $\rho{=}0.326$, comparable to constrained results (Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}).
The failure to improve selection despite reduced compression is consistent with CoNLL's low oracle headroom (5.0~pp at $N{=}8$), which limits the selection space regardless of score distribution quality.

\section{LP Selection Failure Stability}\label{app:lp_failure_stability}

We analyze RE LP selection failures across three random seeds (constrained decoding, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$, Qwen3-8B) to assess whether failures are systematic or stochastic.

\paragraph{Pairwise overlap.}
LP selection failures (instances where LP-selected F1 $<$ single-sample F1) show moderate cross-seed stability: the average pairwise Jaccard similarity is 0.42 (range: 0.38--0.46); failures are partially systematic (driven by instance complexity) but not fully deterministic.
The 3-way intersection contains 34 instances (27.9\% of any-seed failures), which constitutes a stable failure core.

\paragraph{Instance complexity drives failure.}
Table~\ref{tab:stable_failures} stratifies instances by failure stability.
Stable failures (all 3 seeds) involve more gold relations (2.12 vs.\ 1.62 for never-fail instances) and higher single-sample F1 (0.688 vs.\ 0.429); LP mis-selects on instances where the model already performs well, precisely the instances where selection would be most valuable.
Failure rate increases monotonically with gold relation count: 4.3\% at 1 relation, 20.7\% at 3 relations, 26.2\% at 6 relations.

Only 5 RE instances with gold relations flip from LP failure (constrained) to LP success (free-form), with mean gold relation count 3.67 (well above the population mean of 1.86).

1165	\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
1166	When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
1167	The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (single-sample F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.
1168	
1169	\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
1170	The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
1171	The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
1172	Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
1173	These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.
1174	
1175	\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
1176	The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
1177	This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

1207	VerbConf exhibits extreme score compression: mean confidence is 8.58/10 on SciERC (single-sample F1${=}0.645$) and 9.24/10 on CoNLL (single-sample F1${=}0.904$), with most scores concentrated in the 8--10 range.
1208	This compression is more severe than LP (which spans a 0.041-nat median range); score compression is a general property of model self-assessment, not an artifact of log-probability computation.
1209	
1210	\paragraph{QE--selection decoupling.}
1211	VerbConf achieves higher $\rho$ than LP on both datasets (SciERC: 0.297 vs.\ 0.205; CoNLL: 0.337 vs.\ 0.316) and competitive AUROC (SciERC: 0.681 vs.\ 0.578; CoNLL: 0.747 vs.\ 0.753), yet yields the worst selection among all signals ($\Delta{=}{-}2.45$~pp on SciERC, $-1.93$~pp on CoNLL).
1212	This dissociation further demonstrates the correlation-selection gap: a signal can rank instances by expected quality without being able to discriminate candidates within an instance.
1213	The AUROC--$\rho$ decoupling on CoNLL (LP leads AUROC at 0.753 while VerbConf leads $\rho$ at 0.337) reflects differing sensitivity to binary vs.\ ordinal discrimination.

1346	\section{Calibration Baseline}\label{app:calibration_baseline}
1347	
1348	Standard calibration methods are monotonic transforms of log-probability and therefore preserve within-instance sample rankings: Platt scaling \cite{platt1999probabilistic} fits a logistic regression $\sigma(a \cdot \text{LP} + b)$, and temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} divides logits by a scalar $\tau$.
1349	Since both preserve the argmax, selection F1 is identical to raw LP on all three datasets (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}).
1350	
1351	To break monotonicity, we fit a multi-feature Platt model (MF-Platt) using LP, token count, and entity count as inputs, trained on a held-out calibration split (20\% of the test set, 5-fold cross-validation on the remainder).
1352	MF-Platt can reorder candidates within an instance, yet yields no significant selection improvement: $\Delta{=}{-}1.1$~pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.72$), $+0.3$~pp on CoNLL ($p{=}0.31$), and $-0.6$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{=}0.83$).
1353	Platt scaling substantially improves probability calibration (ECE drops from 0.26--0.39 to 0.01--0.08), but better-calibrated probabilities do not translate to better selection.
1354	This parallels the supervised signal combination result (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}): neither stronger aggregation nor additional features can compensate for weak per-sample discriminative signal.

1374	\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}
1375	
1376	\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
1377	Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
1378	Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
1379	LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
1380	Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.
1381	
1382	Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
1383	Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
1384	This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

1440	\subsection{Degeneracy-Aware LP Selection}\label{app:dals}
1441	
1442	The non-tied subset analysis (Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}) identifies within-instance LP range (max minus min LP across $N$ samples) as a per-instance degeneracy proxy: instances with near-zero LP range carry no discriminative signal.
1443	Degeneracy-aware LP selection (DALS) operationalizes this: when LP range exceeds $\tau{=}0.05$ (the threshold independently motivated by the non-tied analysis; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), select the highest-LP sample; otherwise fall back to greedy.
1444	On SciERC, DALS yields $+0.71{\pm}0.48$~pp (3-seed mean; individual seeds: $+0.19$ to $+1.14$~pp); on Few-NERD, $+0.30$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; gain remains positive across $\tau \in [0.01, 0.15]$); on CoNLL, where pure LP selection degrades F1 ($-0.85$~pp), DALS shows comparable degradation (Qwen: $-0.87$~pp; LLaMA: neutral).
1445	DALS improves over pure LP selection when degeneracy is moderate, provides partial damage control when LP selection is harmful, and defaults to greedy when LP range signals no information.
1446	While gains are modest and seed-sensitive, LP range serves as an operationally accessible degeneracy proxy, though the mixed cross-dataset results confirm that degeneracy gating alone cannot ensure positive selection outcomes.
1447	
1448	\paragraph{LOO $\tau$ sensitivity.}
1449	Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation across datasets reveals that the optimal $\tau$ spans two orders of magnitude: $\tau^*{=}0.001$ on Few-NERD, $0.05$ on SciERC, and $0.10$ on CoNLL.
1450	LOO regret (the gap between oracle and LOO-selected $\tau$) ranges from 0.51 to 1.21~pp.
1451	The best single cross-dataset $\tau$ ($\tau{=}0.05$) matches the independently motivated non-tied threshold, but yields dataset-specific suboptimality: even with oracle $\tau$, CoNLL remains at $-0.31$~pp.
1452	This sensitivity reinforces the diagnostic framing of DALS: per-dataset $\tau$ tuning is required for positive gains, and even optimally tuned DALS cannot overcome weak LP-quality alignment on high-degeneracy datasets.

\paragraph{$N$-scaling: selection headroom vs.\ selection gain.}
Table~\ref{tab:n_scaling_selection} traces the effect of sample count on degeneracy, oracle headroom, and per-signal selection gain.
Oracle headroom grows roughly linearly with $N$ ($+4.4$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $+20.0$~pp at $N{=}32$).
LP selection improves monotonically with $N$ ($+0.39$~pp at $N{=}8$ to $+0.95$~pp at $N{=}32$), but even at $N{=}32$, where degeneracy falls to 4\% and oracle headroom reaches ${\sim}20$~pp, the best signal captures less than 5\% of the available improvement.
Degeneracy drops monotonically (43\% at $N{=}2$ to 4\% at $N{=}32$), yet reduced degeneracy does not unlock selection, consistent with the LoRA-rank ablation finding (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}).
VC selection degrades with increasing $N$ ($-2.66$~pp at $N{=}2$ to $-4.35$~pp at $N{=}32$), consistent with mode-seeking bias in voting-based selection as the candidate pool grows.

\paragraph{Temperature controls degeneracy and LP spread.}
Table~\ref{tab:t_degeneracy} reports instance degeneracy (constant F1, gold-filtered) and median within-instance LP range across four temperatures on SciERC.
Both quantities are strictly monotonic in $T$: degeneracy falls from 41.4\% ($T{=}0.5$) to 14.9\% ($T{=}1.2$), while LP range increases from 0.015 to 0.058 nats.
Temperature thus provides a direct lever for practitioners to shift the degeneracy regime.
However, even at $T{=}1.2$ where degeneracy (14.9\%) approaches Few-NERD levels (${\sim}$14\%), within-instance $\rho(\text{LP}, \text{F1})$ remains at 0.225, far below Few-NERD's ${\sim}$0.5.
This confirms that temperature controls degeneracy but cannot improve LP-quality alignment, which is largely determined by task structure and remains relatively stable across generation configurations (\S\ref{app:epoch_confound}). LP-quality alignment, not degeneracy, is the primary predictor of LP selection direction (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).

\paragraph{Wider-to-narrower schema transfer.}
When the SciERC-trained model (6 NER types) is applied to CoNLL (4 types), all signals remain significant ($p{<}0.001$) and structural signals improve over their in-domain levels (same model, seed${=}42$, $N{=}8$; in-domain $\rho$ from Table~\ref{tab:quality_estimation}): VC reaches $\rho{=}0.469$ (in-domain $0.379$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.090$), SJ $\rho{=}0.378$ (in-domain $0.360$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$), and FK $\rho{=}0.285$ (in-domain $0.267$, $\Delta{=}{+}0.018$).
The wider training schema subsumes CoNLL's narrower schema, so the model produces reasonable outputs even out-of-domain (single-sample F1${=}0.522$), and structural signals benefit from the simpler target schema's reduced output ambiguity.

\paragraph{Narrower-to-wider schema transfer (excluded).}
The reverse direction is excluded from our conclusions due to catastrophic model failure, not signal failure.
The CoNLL-trained model recognizes only 4 news entity types (PER, ORG, LOC, MISC) and has no relation extraction capability; when applied to SciERC's 6 scientific entity types and 7 relation types, the model cannot produce meaningful structured outputs (single-sample NER F1${=}0.009$, RE F1${=}0.001$).
Under this regime, most signals flip to negative or near-zero correlations (Table~\ref{tab:ood}); only VC retains weak positive correlation ($\rho{=}0.105$, $p{=}0.016$).
These negative correlations reflect the model systematically generating confident but incorrect outputs, a capability failure analogous to WNUT-17 (\S\ref{sec:qe_results}) and not evidence against signal utility.

\paragraph{Asymmetry interpretation.}
The directional asymmetry is driven by schema coverage: wider$\to$narrower preserves signal utility because the SciERC model's 6-type schema subsumes CoNLL's 4 types, while narrower$\to$wider fails because the CoNLL model lacks the entity and relation types required by SciERC.
This extends the capability boundary identified on WNUT-17 to the domain-shift setting: confidence signals require sufficient model capability as a prerequisite, and results from the CoNLL$\to$SciERC direction should not be interpreted as evidence of signal degradation under domain shift.

\paragraph{QE--selection decoupling.}

The AUROC--$\rho$ decoupling on CoNLL (LP leads AUROC at 0.753 while VerbConf leads $\rho$ at 0.337) reflects differing sensitivity to binary vs.\ ordinal discrimination.

\section{Calibration Baseline}\label{app:calibration_baseline}

Standard calibration methods are monotonic transforms of log-probability and therefore preserve within-instance sample rankings: Platt scaling \cite{platt1999probabilistic} fits a logistic regression $\sigma(a \cdot \text{LP} + b)$, and temperature scaling \cite{guo2017calibration} divides logits by a scalar $\tau$.
Since both preserve the argmax, selection F1 is identical to raw LP on all three datasets (Table~\ref{tab:calibration}).

To break monotonicity, we fit a multi-feature Platt model (MF-Platt) using LP, token count, and entity count as inputs, trained on a held-out calibration split (20\% of the test set, 5-fold cross-validation on the remainder).
MF-Platt can reorder candidates within an instance, yet yields no significant selection improvement: $\Delta{=}{-}1.1$~pp on SciERC ($p{=}0.72$), $+0.3$~pp on CoNLL ($p{=}0.31$), and $-0.6$~pp on Few-NERD ($p{=}0.83$).
Platt scaling substantially improves probability calibration (ECE drops from 0.26--0.39 to 0.01--0.08), but better-calibrated probabilities do not translate to better selection.
This parallels the supervised signal combination result (\S\ref{sec:robustness_main}): neither stronger aggregation nor additional features can compensate for weak per-sample discriminative signal.

\section{Epoch Confound Analysis}\label{app:epoch_confound}

\paragraph{Training convergence modulates degeneracy.}
Table~\ref{tab:epoch_confound} compares the 3-epoch model (used throughout the main text) with a 5-epoch variant on Few-NERD (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$).
Extended training increases greedy F1 by $+2.95$~pp (0.748 $\to$ 0.777) but nearly triples instance degeneracy (11.1\% $\to$ 31.3\%), reducing the fraction of instances with non-degenerate outputs from 85.6\% to 68.7\%.
LP selection gains drop correspondingly ($+1.37$~pp $\to$ $+0.62$~pp), consistent with the degeneracy-gating mechanism identified in the main text (\S\ref{sec:discussion}).
Within-instance LP-quality alignment is relatively stable under this convergence shift (mean $\rho$: $0.524 \to 0.407$; median $\rho$: $0.667 \to 0.615$), consistent with alignment being determined primarily by task structure rather than training duration.

Evaluation loss increases after epoch 3 (0.032 $\to$ 0.041 at epoch 5), and the best checkpoint by validation loss occurs at step 32{,}000 (approximately epoch 3.9).
Standard early stopping practice thus naturally selects the low-degeneracy regime where LP selection is most effective.
This finding refines the narrative: degeneracy is not a fixed property of datasets but is modulated by the degree of training convergence. Over-trained models compress their output distributions, collapsing diversity even on datasets that support it under well-regularized training.

\subsection{Degeneracy-Aware LP Selection}\label{app:dals}

The non-tied subset analysis (Table~\ref{tab:nontied_main}) identifies within-instance LP range (max minus min LP across $N$ samples) as a per-instance degeneracy proxy: instances with near-zero LP range carry no discriminative signal.
Degeneracy-aware LP selection (DALS) operationalizes this: when LP range exceeds $\tau{=}0.05$ (the threshold independently motivated by the non-tied analysis; Appendix~\ref{app:epsilon_robustness}), select the highest-LP sample; otherwise fall back to greedy.
On SciERC, DALS yields $+0.71{\pm}0.48$~pp (3-seed mean; individual seeds: $+0.19$ to $+1.14$~pp); on Few-NERD, $+0.30$~pp ($p{<}0.001$; gain remains positive across $\tau \in [0.01, 0.15]$); on CoNLL, where pure LP selection degrades F1 ($-0.85$~pp), DALS shows comparable degradation (Qwen: $-0.87$~pp; LLaMA: neutral).
DALS improves over pure LP selection when degeneracy is moderate, provides partial damage control when LP selection is harmful, and defaults to greedy when LP range signals no information.
While gains are modest and seed-sensitive, LP range serves as an operationally accessible degeneracy proxy, though the mixed cross-dataset results confirm that degeneracy gating alone cannot ensure positive selection outcomes.

\paragraph{LOO $\tau$ sensitivity.}
Leave-one-out (LOO) cross-validation across datasets reveals that the optimal $\tau$ spans two orders of magnitude: $\tau^*{=}0.001$ on Few-NERD, $0.05$ on SciERC, and $0.10$ on CoNLL.
LOO regret (the gap between oracle and LOO-selected $\tau$) ranges from 0.51 to 1.21~pp.
The best single cross-dataset $\tau$ ($\tau{=}0.05$) matches the independently motivated non-tied threshold, but yields dataset-specific suboptimality: even with oracle $\tau$, CoNLL remains at $-0.31$~pp.
This sensitivity reinforces the diagnostic framing of DALS: per-dataset $\tau$ tuning is required for positive gains, and even optimally tuned DALS cannot overcome weak LP-quality alignment on high-degeneracy datasets.

\subsection{Entity-Level Majority Voting}\label{app:entity_merge}

Entity-level majority voting constructs a merged output by including all (text, type) entity tuples that appear in at least $k$ of $N$ samples (with $k = N/2$ as the default majority threshold).
Unlike best-of-$N$ selection (which picks one complete sample), merge combines evidence across samples at entity granularity.
We sweep $k \in \{2, 3, \ldots, 8\}$ on each dataset (Qwen3-8B, $N{=}8$, $T{=}1.0$) and report the best threshold per dataset.

content.text:
审计完成。47 条定量 claim，38 条验证通过。关键发现：

**HIGH（必须修）：**

| ID | 问题 | 位置 | 修复 |
|---|---|---|---|
| INC-01 | **"ρ up to 0.50" 无支撑** — 所有配置最大 ρ ≈ 0.48（LLaMA CoNLL N=16 SJ），N=8 主表最大 0.451 | abstract, intro×2, conclusion, fig_overview caption（共 5 处） | 改为 "ρ up to 0.48" 或 "ρ up to 0.45"（仅 N=8） |
| UPD-01 | **Few-NERD N=16 LP "+0.52pp" 无来源** — 引用 Appendix app:n_scaling，但该节只有 SciERC 数据；registry exp_027 显示 5K 子集 +1.88pp，与 0.52pp 不一致 | experiments.tex:143 | 补充 Few-NERD N=16 全测试集数据到附录，或更正数值 |

**MEDIUM：**

| ID | 问题 | 修复 |
|---|---|---|
| INC-04 | fig_selection_gap caption 说 "ρ up to 0.36"，但 SciERC VC ρ=.379 | 检查图是否包含 VC；如包含则改为 "up to 0.38" |
| INC-05 | Discussion T=1.2 用 mean ρ=0.225，但其他地方用 median（Table within_rho） | 统一为 median（0.315）或标注 "mean" |
| UPD-02 | Few-NERD N=16 construction "+1.32pp" 同样引用 app:n_scaling 但该节无此数据 | 补充数据到附录 |

**LOW：** oracle headroom 13.0 vs 13.1pp 取整不一致；SciERC greedy F1 枚举缺 .646；FK dependence range −0.4%~−4.0% 在附录中无对应数据。

报告已写入 `artifacts/claim_audit_v2.json`。
